value: The accused was charged with trespassing into the house of a woman and assaulting her with intent to outrage her modesty. The evidence, however, indicated that the accused had assaulted the woman's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty. The accused defended himself against the charge of assaulting the woman and focused his cross-examination on proving that he did not assault or outrage the modesty of the woman. The prosecution's case was that the accused had touched and caught the hand of the daughter-in-law and fled when she raised an alarm. The trial court convicted the accused under sections 452 and 354 of the IPC, but the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, held that the charge was incorrect as it did not mention the daughter-in-law, and the accused was not aware of the charge against her. The Court concluded that the accused was prejudiced by the error in the charge and directed a new trial after framing a charge against the daughter-in-law.

value: The case involves a dispute between Indian Explosives Limited (IEL) and Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited (FCIL). FCIL entered into a tripartite agreement with IEL and Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL) to supply ammonium nitrate to IEL in exchange for explosives. Due to financial difficulties and a breakdown of equipment, FCIL could not fulfill its obligations. FCIL was declared a sick company by the Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) and was directed to be wound up. IEL filed a criminal complaint against senior functionaries of FCIL, alleging cheating and criminal breach of trust under Sections 420, 406, and 1208 of the IPC, as well as Sections 540 and 542 of the Companies Act. The magistrate took cognizance of the complaint and issued summons against the accused. The accused filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the summons, which was dismissed by the High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the magistrate's order, finding no prima facie case against the accused.

The deceased was found in her bedroom with signs of violence, including ligature marks and burn injuries. The accused were found to have committed the crime, with the mother-in-law falsely reporting the death as a suicide. The prosecution established that the accused caused the death through strangulation and burning, which was a case of dowry death.

value: The accused, a man, assaulted his wife with a chopper on her neck in their bedroom, resulting in her death. The victim's body was discovered by neighbors, covered in blood. The accused was seen by witnesses carrying a blood-stained chopper and his 8-month-old son. The medical examination of the victim's body confirmed injuries consistent with the weapon seized from the accused. The accused claimed insanity due to paranoid schizophrenia, but the courts found no evidence he was mentally ill at the time of the crime. The accused had a history of treatment for a psychotic disorder in 1985, but there was no indication of mental illness post-1985. The accused's actions, including leaving the child with a neighbor and confessing to the crime, suggested he understood the nature of his actions.

value: The prosecution case was that on the fateful day, accused persons equipped with deadly weapons reached the spot of occurrence and started inflicting injuries on the deceased and others. Thereafter, the accused persons fled away. The police van reached the spot and removed the deceased to the hospital where he was declared dead. A Parcha Bayan was lodged by a witness who was the brother of the deceased. The prosecution examined 33 witnesses and presented evidence of injuries found on the deceased's body. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the accused under Sections 148, 201, and 302 of the IPC. The High Court set aside the conviction under Sections 148 and 201 but upheld the conviction under Section 302. The Supreme Court, however, found that the evidence of the brother of the deceased, who was a highly interested witness, was not reliable. value: The accused, an army official, was charged with the murder of his colleague. According to the prosecution, the accused reported to his superior officer that the deceased and another individual had abused him. After making the complaint, the accused went to the barrack with a kitchen knife concealed in his lungi and stabbed the deceased on the right side of his chest while the deceased was sleeping. The eyewitness to the incident was present and witnessed the stabbing. The deceased succumbed to the injuries. The accused was initially sentenced to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment and dismissed from service. The sentence was later revised to life imprisonment and dismissal from service. The accused challenged the conviction and sentence, arguing that the incident was due to grave and sudden provocation and that the offense fell under Section 304 (Part II) of the IPC. The High Court rejected these arguments, finding that the accused had sufficient time to deliberate and plan the attack, and that the use of a sharp weapon on a vital part of the body indicated an intention to cause death.

value: The prosecution case was that a dead body was found in a house in Delhi. The dead body was identified as the husband of PW-23. The wife of the deceased stated that her husband had in possession a licensed revolver, a mobile phone SIM (9871879824), and a sum of Rs.3 lakhs when he left Chandigarh for Delhi to negotiate a settlement. During the investigation, it was found that the mobile phone (9871879824) was used on a mobile handset bearing IMEI no.35136304044030. Further investigation revealed that the said IMEI was used for the mobile phone SIM 9818480558 belonging to the accused-appellant immediately after the murder of the victim-deceased. This helped the police in apprehending the appellant and in recovery of three mobile handsets, one of which bore the IMEI no.35136304044030. The police also recovered from the appellant, the licensed revolver of the deceased. The amount of Rs.3 lakhs was not found, however, there was a deposit entry in the account of the appellant of Rs.9000 two days after the murder. Based on circumstantial evidence, the trial court convicted the appellant under Sections 302 and 404 IPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs.50000 for the offence punishable under Section 302, IPC. The appellant was also sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay Rs5000 for offence punishable under Section 404, IPC. He was, however, acquitted of the charges framed against him under Sections 380 and 452, IPC. The High Court dismissed the appeal against conviction, however, modified the sentence inasmuch as in the event of non-payment of fine imposed on the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 302, IPC, the High Court reduced the period of imprisonment in lieu thereof from three years to six months.

value: The prosecution case was that two appellants, along with another accused, caused the death of the victim by assaulting him with sharp edged weapons. The victim was taken to the hospital where he was examined by a doctor and declared dead. The accused were arrested, and the weapons used in the crime were recovered on their disclosure statements. value: The prosecution case is that the deceased had constructed some shop on his land. The accused were charged under s. 302, 201, 379, 411 rlw. s. 34 IPC. The prosecution has proved the complete chain of events, including the last seen together theory, the strangulation of the deceased by the accused, and the disposal of the body in gunny bags into a van. value: The prosecution alleged that on the fateful day, a police officer witnessed three individuals chasing another person. The chased individual fell on the road and was stabbed by the three individuals. The police officer, who was on a motorcycle, could not stop the assailants and they fled. The police officer then took the victim to the hospital where he was declared dead. The police officer checked the victim's pockets and found an identity card, which led to the victim's identification. The police officer then lodged a complaint, and an FIR was filed. The investigating officer examined witnesses and recovered weapons, which were sent for forensic analysis. The trial court acquitted the accused, and the High Court initially convicted one of the accused. The Supreme Court reviewed the case, noting the lack of reliable evidence, the absence of corroborating witnesses, and the unreliability of the sole eyewitness, the police officer. The Supreme Court ultimately acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case to be improbable and lacking in credibility.

value: The accused was prosecuted for the murder and rape of a minor girl aged between 5 and 6 years. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was raped and killed by the accused while she was sleeping in the house of the accused with her blind grandmother. The post-mortem report indicated that the deceased died due to shock and hemorrhage resulting from ante-mortem vaginal injuries. The trial court acquitted the accused, while the High Court convicted him. The accused contended that there was no evidence to establish that the deceased slept in his house or that he had the opportunity to commit the offense. The High Court, however, reversed the acquittal, finding that the trial court had misappreciated the evidence and caused a miscarriage of justice. The prosecution relied on witness testimonies, medical evidence, and the recovery of items with blood and semen, which the trial court had discounted. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, emphasizing that the trial court had given undue weight to discrepancies and inconsistencies, leading to an unjust acquittal.

value: The accused, the husband of the deceased, was charged with causing the death of his wife, who died of burn injuries within seven years of their marriage. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment by her in-laws in connection with dowry demands from the initial days of her marriage. It was stated that the in-laws had previously attempted to set her ablaze, but later assured her parents they would not harass her. The deceased was found dead from extensive burn injuries. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 304B IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The High Court, however, converted the conviction to Section 306 IPC and reduced the sentence to five years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 1000. The court noted that while there was evidence of cruelty and harassment, there was no specific evidence that the accused demanded dowry, and thus the presumption of dowry death could not be drawn. However, the court found that the accused's actions led to the deceased's suicidal death, and thus the conviction under Section 306 IPC was upheld.

value: The accused, the husband of the deceased, was charged with causing the death of his wife, who died from burn injuries. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to physical and mental torture by her husband and in-laws for not providing sufficient dowry. The accused claimed that his wife had left behind a suicide note stating that she committed suicide due to harassment by her parents, not by her husband or in-laws. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 304 and 498A of the IPC, citing harassment and cruelty. The High Court acquitted two other relatives but upheld the conviction of the accused. The Supreme Court reviewed the case, noting that the demand for Rs.50,000/- by the accused for a computer was not a dowry demand as it was not connected to the marriage. The court also found that the suicide note, written by the deceased, cast doubt on the prosecution's claim of harassment and cruelty. The court ultimately acquitted the accused, stating that the prosecution failed to prove the essential ingredients of the offenses beyond reasonable doubt.

value: The accused, a husband and his mother-in-law, were charged with the murder of the deceased, who was their wife. The prosecution alleged that the accused harassed the deceased for dowry and set her on fire. The deceased provided a dying declaration stating that her husband scolded her for not bringing money for her sister's marriage, demanded money from her father, and that her in-laws harassed her for dowry. The deceased was taken to the hospital, where she was examined by a doctor and a Judicial Magistrate recorded her dying declaration. The accused were arrested, and a stove containing kerosene was recovered. The deceased later succumbed to her injuries. The trial court convicted the accused based on the dying declaration and medical evidence, and the High Court upheld the conviction.

value: The accused was prosecuted for rape. The prosecution alleged that the accused committed rape on the prosecutrix. The prosecutrix immediately after returning home narrated the incident to her mother-in-law. One day after the incident, when her husband returned home, she lodged an FIR. The medical report did not give a definite opinion on whether she suffered sexual intercourse, but the FSL report confirmed spots of semen and spermatozoa on her petticoat. The trial court acquitted the accused on the ground that sexual intercourse was with the consent of the prosecutrix. The High Court convicted the accused. The prosecutrix stated that the accused fell her down, covered her mouth, restricted her hands, and committed rape. The FIR and evidence of the prosecutrix's mother-in-law corroborated her statement. The FSL report confirmed sexual intercourse. The accused did not present a defense of consent and claimed he was falsely implicated due to a quarrel with the prosecutrix's husband, but this defense was not supported by evidence.

value: The accused was charged with offences punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of the Indian Penal Code. To prove he was a juvenile at the time of the incident, he submitted a school leaving certificate issued by the Principal of a school. The certificate indicated his date of birth as 10.05.1991. The accused provided testimony from the Head Mistress of the school, who confirmed the authenticity of the certificate. The respondent contested the certificate, leading to an enquiry by the Juvenile Justice Board. The Board sought the opinion of a Medical Board, which opined the accused was approximately 20 years old at the time of the incident. The Sessions Judge set aside the JJ Board's order, directing the case back to the JJ Board for trial. The High Court restored the JJ Board's order, but the Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, reinstating the Sessions Judge's order. The Supreme Court concluded that the school leaving certificate was valid and that the accused was a juvenile at the time of the incident, thus the case should be tried by the JJ Board.

value: The accused was alleged to have committed rape on a minor girl. The victim, who was 17 years old at the time of the incident, attempted suicide after the alleged rape and later disclosed the incident to her family and the police. The victim's family reported the case to the police, leading to the registration of an FIR. The victim underwent medical examination, and the medical report indicated that her hymen was intact. The accused was arrested and charged under Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted the accused and sentenced him to seven years of rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 5,000. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence. The accused appealed, arguing that the delay in lodging the FIR and the medical evidence undermined the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court examined the evidence, including the victim's testimony, the delay in reporting the incident, and the trauma experienced by the victim. The Court found the prosecution's case credible, noting that the delay in reporting the incident and the victim's suicide attempt supported her account of the rape. The Court also emphasized that the amendment to Section 114-A of the Evidence Act supported the prosecution's case, even in the absence of clear medical evidence of rape.

value: The prosecution case was that on 25.11.2003, the accused's husband returned home from a clinic and found a servant, aged 13 years, weeping. The accused fled after the assault, and one of them took the servant to the terrace and instructed him to falsely accuse thieves. value: The accused, the husband of the victim, subjected the victim to cruelty and harassment in connection with a demand for dowry. Nine months after their marriage, the victim sustained burn injuries. The next day, she made a dying declaration before a magistrate, initially stating it was an accident, but later alleging that her husband had doused her in kerosene and set her on fire. The prosecution presented evidence including the victim's dying declaration, the testimony of the victim's parents, and a medical report indicating the cause of death was burns. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC, and the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction, finding that the evidence supported the prosecution's case of dowry death and harassment.

value: The accused, who were the husband and brothers of the deceased, were charged with her death. The deceased married the accused shortly before her death. The deceased died in the accused's house, and the post-mortem examination revealed severe burn injuries. The prosecution presented circumstantial evidence indicating that the deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment in connection with dowry demands. The deceased's family members testified that the accused had been taunting her and demanding dowry. The medical examination showed that the deceased had consumed toxic substances before her death. The accused were convicted based on the circumstantial evidence, which formed a complete chain of circumstances linking them to the crime. The accused claimed that the deceased committed suicide, but the court rejected this claim, finding that the circumstantial evidence did not support such a conclusion.

During the High Court's appeal, a compromise was reached between the parties, leading to a reduction in the sentence and an increase in compensation.

value: The accused persons, who were armed with weapons, approached the victim and another individual near a cycle stand at a college campus. They demanded that the victim and the other individual withdraw their names from a college election. When they refused, the accused assaulted them. The victim sustained severe injuries and later succumbed to his injuries. The other individual also received injuries and lodged a complaint with the police. The prosecution presented eyewitness accounts, medical reports, and statements from witnesses to establish that the victim died as a result of the assault. The accused were present at the scene and participated in the attack, with specific roles in causing injuries to the victim. The investigation had some flaws, such as the non-recovery of weapons and delayed recovery of a blood-stained shirt, but the medical evidence and testimonies of the prosecution witnesses supported the prosecution's case. The accused were found to have formed an unlawful assembly with the common object of preventing the victim from contesting the election, and the circumstances indicated that a common intention to kill may have arisen on the spur of the moment.

value: The accused were involved in a dispute with the victim's family over land and water rights. The victim was caught by the accused, his hands were tied behind his back, and he was assaulted with a club of stone, resulting in injuries to his head and other parts of his body. The victim died as a result of these injuries. The prosecution relied on the statements of the victim's brother and mother, who claimed to be eyewitnesses. However, their conduct was deemed unnatural as they did not intervene during the assault and left the victim to die without providing assistance. The investigating officer admitted to destroying the initial report provided by the victim's brother, which undermined the prosecution's case. The trial court found the prosecution's evidence unreliable and acquitted the accused, while the High Court overturned this decision. The Supreme Court reviewed the case and ultimately acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's version of events to be inconsistent and unreliable.

value: The accused, a male, and his co-accused, a female, were charged with the murder of the victim, a male. The victim's body was found hanging from the roof of a shed adjacent to his house. The sole eyewitness, PW1, claimed to have witnessed the incident, which he described as occurring between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. on the night of 19/20 February 2000. PW1 stated that the accused assaulted the victim from behind, causing him to fall, and then sat on his chest, throttling him while the co-accused covered the victim's mouth. The accused then tied a rope around the victim's neck and suspended his body from the shed. PW1 also alleged an extra-marital relationship between the accused and the co-accused, which was presented as the motive for the murder. The medical evidence indicated that the victim died from asphyxia due to neck constriction, not from hanging. The incident was initially registered as an unnatural death but was later converted into a murder case after six days. The prosecution relied on PW1's testimony, as well as the testimonies of PW5, PW6, and PW8, who learned of the incident from PW1. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302 IPC, relying on PW1's account and the medical evidence. The High Court affirmed the conviction, accepting the prosecution's claim of motive based on the extra-marital relationship. However, the Supreme Court found PW1's testimony to be unreliable, inconsistent, and improbable, leading to the acquittal of the accused.

value: The accused, along with others, were present at a tube well where the deceased was found dead. The accused were armed with weapons and fled the scene after the incident. value: The accused and the deceased were involved in a dispute over the sale of property. On the day of the incident, the accused and his father arrived at the office of a third party where the deceased and his brothers were already present. An altercation occurred between the accused and the deceased, leading to a scuffle. During the scuffle, the deceased and his brothers attempted to strangle the accused. The accused reached for his revolver, and upon seeing the gun, the deceased released him and started running. The accused then fired the shot, which hit the deceased from behind. The bullet entered the body below the right shoulder and traveled upwards without exiting. The medical evidence indicated that the shot was fired from a distant range, and there was no blackening or charring around the wound. The accused was convicted of murder, but the conviction was later overturned on the grounds that the accused acted in self-defense without premeditation.

value: The accused borrowed a total of Rs. 64,000 from the complainant and issued three cheques, two of which were returned by the bank as dishonoured. The complainant received an intimation from the bank about the dishonour of the cheques on 08.04.1991. The complainant issued a legal notice to the accused on 12.04.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating the addressee was absent. The complainant sent another legal notice on 04.05.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating it was refused. The complainant then filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Trial Court convicted the accused, and the Appellate Court upheld the conviction. The High Court reversed the conviction, arguing that the second notice was sent beyond the 15-day limit. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, finding that the first notice was valid and the second notice was merely a reminder.

value: The accused, a group of sixteen individuals, were alleged to have assaulted and killed the deceased during a dispute over money. The deceased's wife, who was the primary witness, claimed that the accused entered her home, dragged the deceased out, and assaulted him, eventually cutting off his right hand. The deceased's body was found in a field without his hand. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements and recovered weapons. However, the witnesses provided inconsistent accounts, and there were no independent witnesses to corroborate the prosecution's case. The medical evidence did not support the claim that the deceased's hand was amputated by the accused. The trial court acquitted the accused due to the lack of conclusive evidence, and the High Court reversed this decision. The Supreme Court reviewed the case and found that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, leading to the restoration of the trial court's acquittal.

value: The prosecution alleges that on May 25, 1994, at approximately 2 pm, the accused were seen beating the victim with lathis. Two eyewitnesses, who were returning from a village, reported the incident and fled due to threats from the accused. They later filed an FIR at the police station. The trial court and high court relied heavily on the testimonies of these two witnesses, which were considered credible. However, the Supreme Court found contradictions in the testimonies of these witnesses, as well as inconsistencies in the FIR and site plan. The investigation was deemed unfair, and the witnesses had criminal antecedents. The court also noted that the witnesses had changed their statements over time, raising doubts about their reliability. The court concluded that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently supported by the evidence and that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the accused.

value: The prosecution case is that six persons, heavily armed with two of them carrying firearms, killed the victim in broad daylight between 12 and 12:30 p.m. The victim was present at the scene and was surrounded by the accused. The accused, including two individuals with firearms, fired multiple shots, resulting in multiple firearm entry wounds as confirmed by medical evidence. The victim died as a result of these injuries. The accused threatened the villagers present at the scene and then fled. The medical report corroborates the prosecution's account of the injuries caused by firearms and sharp-edged weapons. The trial court acquitted the accused, but the High Court overturned this decision, finding the medical evidence supported the eyewitness accounts. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, concluding that the eyewitnesses' statements were credible and corroborated by the medical evidence.

value: The accused, two male individuals, were involved in a case where the victim, a female, was found dead in her home. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the testimony of a child witness, recovery of items such as a motorcycle and a silver anklet, fingerprint reports, and a forensic science laboratory (FSL) report. The child witness's testimony was not corroborated by other witnesses, and there were inconsistencies in the evidence. The prosecution also relied on the recovery of items and the last seen theory, but the evidence was deemed unreliable due to lack of corroboration and inconsistencies. The trial court convicted the accused and sentenced them to death, but the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, found the evidence insufficient and acquitted the accused.

value: The accused, who was employed as a manager in a nationalized bank, was involved in an incident where a savings account was opened in the name of a person, with forged signatures. The account was used to encash a refund cheque. The investigation revealed that the accused had forged the signature of the allottee on the account opening form. A forensic science laboratory report was obtained to analyze the handwriting on the documents. The accused applied for discharge on the grounds that he was a public servant and that prosecution sanction was required under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court rejected the application, and the accused challenged the decision in the High Court. The High Court upheld the trial court's decision, and the Supreme Court affirmed this, noting that the accused was not a public servant removable from his office without government sanction, and therefore, Section 197 did not apply. The court deleted the trial court's observation that the accused had committed forgery, as it was premature to make such a conclusion before trial.

value: The accused, a man, was involved in an incident where he and his wife had a quarrel. The wife attempted to take money from his wallet, which led to a confrontation. The accused picked up a 'saria' (a type of iron rod) and used it to strangle his wife, resulting in her death. The incident occurred on the rooftop of their residence. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the accused's son, who was present at the scene, as well as other witnesses who confirmed the accused's presence and actions. The accused was initially convicted of murder under Section 302 of the IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment. However, the High Court and the Supreme Court reviewed the case, considering whether the act fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, which would reduce the charge to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II. The Supreme Court ultimately modified the conviction and imposed a sentence of 10 years' simple imprisonment.

value: The accused appellant and the main accused were related to each other. There was a previous enmity between them over a land dispute. On the day of the incident, the accused appellant stopped the victim on his way and told him not to cultivate his land. A quarrel started between the victim and the accused appellant. The main accused intervened, whereupon the victim told him not to interfere and to go home as he was not involved in the dispute. The main accused took out a pistol from his pocket and pointed it at the victim. The victim told the main accused not to open fire, whereupon the accused appellant urged the main accused to kill the victim. The main accused then fired the pistol, causing injury to the victim with splinters. The prosecution alleged that the accused appellant instigated the main accused to kill the victim. However, the court found that the prosecution failed to establish a pre-arranged common intention between the accused appellant and the main accused to kill the victim. The court also noted discrepancies in the evidence of the victim and other witnesses, raising doubts about the truth and accuracy of their accounts. The court concluded that the accused appellant did not carry arms or open fire and that the main accused acted on his own initiative.

The accused challenged the conviction before the Armed Forces Tribunal, which dismissed the appeal. The accused had served more than 14 years of his sentence and had excellent conduct in jail.

value: The accused, along with two other individuals, attacked the victim while he was walking with his two brothers towards a taxi stand. The accused used hockey sticks and a knife to assault the victim. The victim's brothers attempted to intervene but were threatened by the accused. The victim was taken to the hospital and declared dead. The prosecution relied on the testimony of one eyewitness, who claimed the incident lasted five minutes. value: The accused, a police officer, entered the residential office of the victim in an inebriated condition. After consuming water, he pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the victim, directing the victim's clerk and steno to leave the room. The accused moved around the table, pulled the lever of the pistol, and prepared to fire. The victim lunged at the accused, causing the bullet to hit the ceiling. Forensic evidence confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the victim's office was fired from the accused's service pistol. The accused claimed an alternate version of events, but the trial court found it dubious. value: The case involves an individual who was detained under the National Security Act, 1980. The detention order was initially passed on May 11, 2021, and the individual was detained on May 12, 2021. The order was approved by the State Government on May 13, 2021. The individual submitted a representation against the detention order on May 18, 2021, which was communicated to the State Government and Central Government on May 20, 2021. The Central Government received the representation on June 1, 2021, and the State Government received it on May 24, 2021. The Central Government rejected the representation on June 24, 2021, and the State Government rejected it on July 15, 2021. The individual was not informed of the rejection of the representation until it was communicated to him on June 28, 2021. The Supreme Court held that the delay in considering the representation and the failure to communicate the rejection of the representation violated the individual's constitutional rights under Article 22(5) of the Constitution. The order of detention was therefore invalidated.

value: The accused, who were four brothers, were involved in a dispute over the management of a brick-kiln. The prosecution alleged that they murdered six individuals at different locations within a house. The victims included the accused's father, mother, brother, sister-in-law, nephew, and niece. The prosecution relied on the testimonies of two witnesses, who were closely related to both the accused and the deceased. These witnesses described the events, including the locations where the victims were killed. However, the court found that the witnesses' testimonies were not reliable enough to support a conviction without additional corroboration. The prosecution also presented evidence of weapons and bloodstained clothes, but the court questioned the credibility of these items due to lack of independent witnesses and inconsistencies in the evidence. The accused were arrested shortly after the incident, but the court found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

value: The accused, Parubai, was living in a house with her husband, Gulab, and his first wife, Mandabai, along with their children. On the night of August 2/3, 2006, a fire broke out in the house, engulfing it in flames. The High Court upheld the conviction, but the Supreme Court overturned it, finding that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and that suspicion alone was insufficient to convict.

value: The accused were tried for the murder of the deceased. The prosecution case was that the deceased, along with PW1 and another person, were traveling in a car when the accused attacked them, causing injury to the deceased on the right shoulder. The deceased then tried to run away and reached a shed, where the accused chased him, entered the shed, and caused further injuries leading to the deceased's death. PW1, an eyewitness, was present in the car during the initial attack and later saw the accused enter the shed and cause injuries to the deceased. PW1's testimony was fully supported and cross-examined, and the court found no reason to disbelieve his account. The prosecution also presented medical evidence and statements from witnesses, though some witnesses contradicted the prosecution's timeline and details. The trial court convicted the accused based on PW1's testimony and the evidence, but the High Court acquitted them, citing inconsistencies in the FIR registration, lack of examination of the original complainant, and contradictions in witness statements. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's acquittal, finding PW1's testimony reliable and sufficient for conviction despite the absence of weapon recovery and some contradictions in the FIR timing.

value: The accused, who was the brother of the deceased, was involved in a violent incident where the deceased suffered fatal injuries. The deceased had a history of alcohol addiction and had previously tormented, abused, and threatened the accused. On the night of the incident, the deceased consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, warning that he would kill him if he did not. The accused, who had attempted suicide by holding live electrical wires, lost self-control due to the sudden and grave provocation from the deceased. The accused inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased using a pick-axe. The accused's actions were deemed to be a result of temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation. The accused was initially convicted under s.302 IPC for murder, but the conviction was converted to s.304 Part I IPC under Exception 1 to s.300 IPC due to the provocation and loss of self-control. The accused was sentenced to imprisonment for 10 years, a fine of Rs. 1,000, or simple imprisonment for six months if the fine was not paid.

value: The prosecution alleged that three individuals, who were police officers on patrol, fired at a scooter carrying the deceased, resulting in his death. The deceased was traveling with two witnesses on a separate scooter. The witnesses claimed that the police officers flashed a torch light at them, causing their scooter to skid, and then fired shots at them, which led to the deceased's death. The witnesses managed to escape and later reported the incident. The prosecution also relied on the presence of empty cartridges at the scene, which were matched to the rifles of the accused. However, the deceased's injuries were caused by a .12 bore weapon, which was not recovered from any of the accused. The trial court found the eyewitness accounts of the witnesses inconclusive and the testimony of one witness unreliable, leading to the acquittal of the accused. The High Court dismissed the appeal, noting that the prosecution failed to establish the identity of the accused as the perpetrators.

value: The accused, a police guard, was posted at a police station where the victim, a constable, was on duty. The victim was using an official telephone for a prolonged period, which prompted the accused to approach him and request him to end the call. During the interaction, the accused's semi-automatic fire carbine became entangled with the chain attached to his belt, resulting in accidental firing of five rounds. The bullets struck the victim in the neck, leading to his death. The prosecution initially alleged intentional firing, but the High Court found the motive unproven. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302, but the Supreme Court overturned that conviction, finding the prosecution failed to establish intent. The Court concluded the accused's negligence in not keeping the weapon's safety mechanism engaged led to the accidental death, making him guilty of a lesser offense under Section 304A.

value: The accused, who were the son and associates of the deceased, were implicated in the death of the deceased, who was found dead by his brother. The prosecution alleged that the accused had a property dispute with the deceased and that the accused fled the scene. The accused were apprehended, and items such as a rusted iron rod and a sweater were recovered. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness testimonies about the accused's presence at the scene and Call Detail Records (CDRs) to establish their location. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court upheld the conviction, but the Supreme Court quashed the conviction, finding that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

value: The prosecution alleged that three individuals assaulted and killed a man during a night incident. value: The accused, a driver, was responsible for transporting a female victim who worked late hours at a company in Bengaluru. The victim left her office at 2:00 a.m. in a company-provided vehicle. The accused informed her that the vehicle on her usual route was unavailable and offered to transport her in his own vehicle. The victim sat in the accused's car. value: The accused and the victim were strangers who engaged in a verbal altercation that escalated into a physical fight. The accused used dangerous weapons, including a sickle and sword, to assault the victim. The victim sustained severe injuries, including bleeding on his head, left paw, wrist, right hand, and right shoulder, and ultimately succumbed to his injuries. The accused claimed the case fell under Exception 4 to Section 300, but the Supreme Court rejected this, emphasizing the use of dangerous weapons and the victim's helplessness.

value: The prosecution alleged that the accused, along with another accused, murdered a woman during the night at the latter's house. The body was discovered in a paddy field by a witness, and a postmortem examination revealed injuries consistent with a violent attack. The prosecution claimed the accused had an illicit relationship with the other accused, which led to the murder. The accused was alleged to have used a coconut scrapper to strike the victim multiple times, dragged the body to the paddy field, and left the scene. The case relied heavily on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements about the accused's presence at the scene, recovery of blood-stained items, and the presence of a weapon. However, the evidence was criticized for gaps and inconsistencies, particularly regarding the accused's presence at the scene and the reliability of recovered items.

value: The case involves a kidnapping and ransom incident where a minor boy was allegedly kidnapped by a group of individuals. The police received secret information about the incident and registered an FIR based on that information. The grandfather of the kidnapped boy was the first to report the incident to the police, but the police did not investigate thoroughly. The prosecution relied on statements from the kidnapped boy and his father, as well as call detail records, to connect the accused to the crime. However, the investigation revealed inconsistencies in the evidence, including the failure to examine the grandfather as a witness, the lack of convincing evidence linking the accused to the mobile numbers used in the crime, and the improper handling of recovered currency notes. The trial court and High Court convicted the accused, but the Supreme Court found the prosecution's case to be fabricated and the conviction to be unsustainable.

value: The prosecution alleged that on 13.11.2011, at 9:30 p.m., the victim, Narayan Singh, was shot dead at his home in Village Binjana, District Dewas, Madhya Pradesh. The victim's mother, Rachna Bai, testified that she and the victim were sleeping when someone called out the victim's name, prompting him to open the door. A gunshot was heard, and shortly after, a second gunshot struck the victim in the chest, causing him to fall. Rachna Bai saw her daughter-in-law and the victim's son standing on the opposite side of the house and two individuals with their faces covered fleeing the scene on a motorcycle. The prosecution's primary evidence against the appellant was the recovery of a pistol from him and a ballistic report confirming that the bullet recovered from the victim's body was fired from the recovered pistol. There were no eyewitnesses to the crime, and the case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence.
